sections.title: Thinking Like a Physicist
sections.learning_target: Students will explain how physics uses observation, measurement, evidence, models, and testable claims to understand the natural world.

i_cans.text: I can distinguish between an observation, inference, hypothesis, law, and theory.
I can explain why a claim must be testable to be scientific.
I can use evidence from a short scenario to decide whether a physics explanation is supported and explain why formulas in physics are guides for thinking, not just tools for calculation.

source_headings: How Eratosthenes Measured the Size of Earth

ordered_flow.source_heading: Scientific Measurements + How Eratosthenes Measured the Size of Earth
ordered_flow.source_block: Measurement as a hallmark of science; one concrete historical measurement/model example.
ordered_flow.purpose: Use one strong case to establish direct measurement, model-based inference, evidence, and the role of quantitative observations.

retained_images.alt_text: Eratosthenes measurement diagram showing Syene, Alexandria, Sun rays, verticals, and 7.1 degree angle.
retained_images.purpose: Use a concrete measurement/model example to separate observations, measurements, inferences, and model-based reasoning.

ordered_flow.concept: Classify observation versus inference from a measurement record.

ordered_flow.discussion_job: Separate what is directly observed from what is inferred from a model.
ordered_flow.prompt_skeleton: Using the measurement figure, identify one direct observation/measurement and one conclusion that requires reasoning beyond what was directly seen.
expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students name a directly measured quantity.
Students distinguish a model-based conclusion from a direct observation.
Students connect evidence to the conclusion rather than treating the diagram as proof by itself.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Size of the Moon / Distance to the Moon / Distance to the Sun / Size of the Sun
ordered_flow.source_block: Extended ancient-astronomy measurement chain, eclipse geometry, pinhole examples, and historical FYI material.
ordered_flow.purpose: Interesting but too long and mostly outside the current Unit 1 targets; retain only the general idea that measurements and models support claims through TB1.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Mathematics—The Language of Science
ordered_flow.source_block: Equations as compact expressions of relationships between physical concepts and as guides to thinking.
ordered_flow.purpose: Directly supports the course emphasis that formulas represent relationships, not answer machines.

ordered_flow.concept: Interpret a physical relationship before calculating.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Scientific Methods
ordered_flow.source_block: Question, hypothesis, prediction, test, and evidence as common features rather than a rigid cookbook method.
ordered_flow.purpose: Preserve the test-evidence logic while cutting long historical framing.

ordered_flow.source_heading: The Scientific Attitude — facts, hypotheses, laws, theories, and evidence
ordered_flow.source_block: Evidence can support, contradict, refine, or replace explanations; scientific terms carry specific meanings.
ordered_flow.purpose: Build the vocabulary distinctions and evidence-based reasoning needed for the exact I-cans.

ordered_flow.concept: Judge which explanation is better supported by evidence.

ordered_flow.source_heading: The Scientific Attitude — testability / falsifiability
ordered_flow.source_block: A scientific claim must be testable in a way that could show it to be wrong.
ordered_flow.purpose: This is the cleanest source block for the exact testable-claim I-can.

ordered_flow.concept: Evaluate whether a claim is testable and identify a measurable test.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Check Points, Check Your Answers, extended opposing-view discussion, footnotes
ordered_flow.source_block: Embedded practice answers and long extensions after the core testability discussion.
ordered_flow.purpose: Canonical Bank EX/YTI replaces this practice; extensions would exceed the lesson-time target.

summary_targets: Measurements and observations provide evidence; inferences and models interpret that evidence.
Hypotheses, laws, and theories have different roles and remain accountable to evidence.
Scientific claims must be testable in principle.
Equations describe relationships among physical quantities and should guide reasoning before calculation.
common_mistakes_targets: Treating an inference as a direct observation.
Assuming a plausible-sounding claim is scientific without a possible test.
Using law and theory as if one simply “graduates” into the other.
Treating a formula as a calculation recipe with no physical meaning.

sections.title: Forces and Newton’s First Law
sections.learning_target: Students will explain Newton’s First Law and use the idea of inertia to predict whether an object’s motion will stay the same or change.

i_cans.text: I can state Newton’s First Law in everyday language.
I can explain that inertia is a property of matter, not a force.
I can distinguish between “no forces acting” and “no net force acting.” and identify support force, weight, and other common forces in simple situations.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Newton’s First Law of Motion
ordered_flow.source_block: Newton’s law of inertia and the key idea that motion continues unless a nonzero net force changes it.
ordered_flow.purpose: Establish the central law in everyday language before examples.

ordered_flow.concept: Apply Newton’s First Law to unchanged motion.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Newton’s First Law of Motion — inertia examples
ordered_flow.source_block: Tablecloth/dishes and related inertia examples.
ordered_flow.purpose: Use one phenomenon-rich visual rather than the full set of demonstrations; emphasize inertia as a property, not a force.

retained_images.alt_text: Figure 2.4: A tablecloth is pulled quickly from beneath dishes on a table.
retained_images.purpose: Anchor inertia as resistance to change in motion without describing inertia as a force.

ordered_flow.concept: Correct the misconception that inertia is a forward force.

ordered_flow.discussion_job: Use an inertia phenomenon to distinguish a tendency to maintain motion from a force that causes change.
ordered_flow.prompt_skeleton: In the tablecloth example, what changes rapidly and what tends to keep its prior state? Explain without calling inertia a force.
expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students use “resists change in motion” or equivalent.
Students do not invent an inertia force.
Students connect a change in motion to net force rather than to motion itself.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Check Point / Check Your Answers after inertia
ordered_flow.source_block: Hockey-puck question plus supplied answer.
ordered_flow.purpose: Canonical Bank anchors already provide aligned prediction/explanation practice.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Personal Essay
ordered_flow.source_block: Extended scaffold autobiography and equilibrium story.
ordered_flow.purpose: Long personal tangent; its useful force-balance idea is taught more directly in Sections 1.2/1.4.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Support Force
ordered_flow.source_block: Book on table: weight downward, support/normal force upward, and zero net force in equilibrium; spring analogy.
ordered_flow.purpose: Directly supports identification of common forces and the distinction between no forces and no net force.

retained_images.alt_text: Figure 2.15: A table pushes up on a book and a spring pushes up on a hand. Downward and upward force arrows are shown.
retained_images.purpose: Make the support-force/weight pair visible and connect balanced nonzero forces to zero net force.

ordered_flow.concept: Identify support force and weight on a chosen object.
Distinguish balanced nonzero forces from no forces acting.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Support Force — bathroom scale extension and Check Point
ordered_flow.source_block: Scale as another support-force example, followed by supplied practice answers.
ordered_flow.purpose: Retain at most one quick scale connection if time allows; omit answer section because Bank practice owns the work.

summary_targets: Newton’s First Law says rest or constant straight-line motion continues when net force is zero.
Inertia is a property of matter that describes resistance to changes in motion; it is not a force.
An object can have several forces acting on it while the net force is zero.
Support force and weight are common forces that can balance on supported objects.
common_mistakes_targets: Saying a moving object needs a net forward force to keep moving at constant velocity.
Calling inertia a force.
Equating zero net force with no forces acting.
Forgetting weight or support force in simple supported-object force models.

sections.title: Net Force and Vectors
sections.learning_target: Students will represent forces as vectors and determine the direction and relative size of the net force in one-dimensional and simple two-dimensional situations.

i_cans.text: I can explain why force is a vector quantity.
I can combine forces acting in the same direction or opposite directions.
I can identify the resultant force from a simple vector diagram and use arrow length and direction to compare force strength and direction.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Net Force and Vectors — combining parallel forces
ordered_flow.source_block: Push/pull, net force, and same-direction/opposite-direction combinations.
ordered_flow.purpose: Establish one-dimensional net force before more formal vector language.

retained_images.alt_text: Figure 2.6: Applied forces combine to produce net forces of 10 N, 0 N, and 5 N.
retained_images.purpose: Show how same- and opposite-direction forces combine and why direction matters.

ordered_flow.concept: Determine directed net force from opposite-direction forces.
Reason backward from a target resultant to a missing force.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Net Force and Vectors — vector vs scalar
ordered_flow.source_block: Force arrows encode both magnitude and direction; arrow length has meaning when drawn to scale.
ordered_flow.purpose: Directly supports vector meaning and reading scaled arrows.

ordered_flow.concept: Interpret magnitude and direction as inseparable features of a force vector.
Read a scaled vector diagram and determine resultant magnitude/direction.

ordered_flow.discussion_job: Use arrow direction and length as evidence before performing arithmetic.
ordered_flow.prompt_skeleton: Without calculating first, which direction should the resultant point in the net-force figure? What visual evidence supports that prediction?
expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students use arrow direction and relative length, not just numbers.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Net Force and Vectors — parallelogram rule
ordered_flow.source_block: Simple two-dimensional addition with a rectangle/parallelogram and diagonal resultant.
ordered_flow.purpose: Keep one clean 2-D representation because the current target includes simple two-dimensional situations.

retained_images.alt_text: Figure 2.8: Perpendicular vectors form a rectangle whose diagonal is the resultant.
retained_images.purpose: Provide one simple two-dimensional resultant model without extending into unnecessary vector mechanics.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Equal perpendicular vectors / square-root-2 extension
ordered_flow.source_block: Special-case geometry and numerical resultant for equal perpendicular vectors.
ordered_flow.purpose: Useful enrichment but not necessary for the current conceptual target or time budget.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Force Vectors — 30-40-50 example
ordered_flow.source_block: One brief example connecting components to a resultant.
ordered_flow.purpose: Preserve the idea of a resultant in two dimensions without turning the lesson into a trigonometry unit.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Nellie rope tensions, omitted-figure notes, appendix/media/footnote extension
ordered_flow.source_block: More complex angled-tension application and reference material.
ordered_flow.purpose: Beyond the section’s simple-vector scope and unnecessary after canonical Bank practice.

summary_targets: A force is a vector because a complete description requires magnitude and direction.
Forces in the same direction add; opposite-direction forces combine by direction-aware subtraction.
The net force/resultant describes the combined effect of all forces on the object.
Scaled arrow length and arrow direction carry physical meaning; a simple 2-D resultant can be represented as a diagonal.
common_mistakes_targets: Adding magnitudes while ignoring direction.
Treating arrow length as decoration.
Reporting a net force magnitude without a direction.
Reversing the resultant direction or choosing the direction of the smaller force.

sections.title: Equilibrium and Balanced Motion
sections.learning_target: Students will determine whether an object is in mechanical equilibrium and explain how balanced forces relate to rest or constant straight-line motion.

i_cans.text: I can recognize static equilibrium and dynamic equilibrium.
I can explain why an object at rest can still have forces acting on it.
I can explain why an object moving at constant speed in a straight line can be in equilibrium and use the equilibrium rule to reason about upward/downward and left/right forces.

textbook_sections: 2.7 source excerpt unavailable in pinned textbook file
source_warnings: The pinned textbook file explicitly notes that cp_section_2_7 source content was unavailable. The target course section itself is present. Dynamic-equilibrium coverage is retained through the Section 2.5 unchanged-motion language, Newton’s First Law connection, the current Assessment Plan, canonical Bank anchors, and an existing course-toolkit constant-speed force figure.

ordered_flow.source_heading: The Equilibrium Rule — hanging bag and definition
ordered_flow.source_block: Equal and opposite nonzero forces; mechanical equilibrium; ΣF = 0.
ordered_flow.purpose: Establish the equilibrium rule and make static equilibrium explicit.

ordered_flow.concept: Recognize static versus dynamic equilibrium.
Explain why an at-rest object can still have forces acting.

ordered_flow.source_heading: The Equilibrium Rule — scaffold force balance
ordered_flow.source_block: Multiple upward and downward vectors balancing to zero.
ordered_flow.purpose: Give a visible multi-force application of ΣF = 0.

retained_images.alt_text: Figure 2.14: Force vectors on a sign-painting scaffold show upward forces balancing downward forces.
retained_images.purpose: Make the equilibrium rule visible through multiple nonzero forces that sum to zero.

ordered_flow.concept: Use equilibrium to determine a missing balancing force and interpret motion.

ordered_flow.source_heading: The Equilibrium Rule — unchanged motion / margin-note bridge
ordered_flow.source_block: Mechanical equilibrium means no change in the state of motion, not “at rest only.”
ordered_flow.purpose: Make the static/dynamic distinction explicit and connect zero net force to constant straight-line motion; pair with the canonical constant-speed force figure because source 2.7 is absent.

retained_images.alt_text: Box moving at constant speed with a push and friction | Constant-speed box force diagram
retained_images.purpose: Supply the missing dynamic-equilibrium representation required by the current I-can: constant straight-line motion with zero net force.

ordered_flow.notes: Extra course figure is justified by the current dynamic-equilibrium I-can and the missing 2.7 source excerpt.

ordered_flow.concept: Check whether constant straight-line motion is consistent with balanced forces.

ordered_flow.discussion_job: Contrast static and dynamic equilibrium using force and motion evidence.
ordered_flow.prompt_skeleton: Compare the scaffold and constant-speed box. What is the same about their net force, and what is different about their motion?
expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students identify zero net force in both cases.
Students distinguish rest from constant straight-line motion.
Students state that equilibrium means unchanged motion, not necessarily zero speed.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Check Point / Check Your Answers
ordered_flow.source_block: Gymnast scale-reading checkpoint and supplied answers.
ordered_flow.purpose: Canonical EX/YTI anchors replace this practice while preserving the equilibrium reasoning.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Practicing Physics / Practicing Physics Answers
ordered_flow.source_block: Three scaffold scale-reading exercises with full answers.
ordered_flow.purpose: Redundant with the canonical Notes examples and would overrun the 30–40 minute target.

summary_targets: Mechanical equilibrium means the net force is zero.
Static equilibrium describes an object at rest with zero net force.
Dynamic equilibrium describes constant straight-line motion with zero net force.
Balanced forces can be nonzero individually; their vector sum is zero.
The equilibrium rule can be used to infer missing upward/downward or left/right forces.
common_mistakes_targets: Equating equilibrium with rest only.
Saying forces disappear when an object is in equilibrium.
Assuming constant speed always means equilibrium even when direction changes.
Balancing magnitudes without checking opposite directions.

sections.title: Modeling Forces in the Real World
sections.learning_target: Students will create and critique force models for real-world situations involving inertia, support force, net force, and equilibrium.

i_cans.text: I can draw a force diagram for an object in a real-world situation.
I can decide whether the forces are balanced or unbalanced.
I can explain how the net force affects the object’s motion and critique an incorrect force explanation and revise it using physics vocabulary.

source_warnings: The pinned textbook identifies this as a synthesis/application section with no single corresponding source-textbook passage. Its existing course-textbook synthesis is used as the instructional spine; no new parallel narrative is invented in 4A.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Putting Force Ideas to Work — toolkit recap
ordered_flow.source_block: Connect inertia/Newton’s First Law, vectors/net force, and equilibrium as one force-modeling toolkit.
ordered_flow.purpose: Activate the conceptual pieces students must combine in the synthesis section.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Putting Force Ideas to Work — three-step modeling process
ordered_flow.source_block: Identify forces on the chosen system, represent them as vectors, then decide whether net force is zero or nonzero and connect that to motion.
ordered_flow.purpose: Provide the section’s core modeling routine without turning it into a formula procedure.

ordered_flow.concept: Define the system and include only forces acting on that object.
Decide whether represented forces are balanced or unbalanced.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Putting Force Ideas to Work — real situations are messy
ordered_flow.source_block: Constant-velocity cart/friction and hanging-sign examples as reminders that visible motion alone does not reveal all individual forces.
ordered_flow.purpose: Use one or two quick contexts to connect the model to evidence without repeating earlier sections.

ordered_flow.concept: Use net-force direction to predict motion change.

ordered_flow.source_heading: Putting Force Ideas to Work — critique and revise models
ordered_flow.source_block: Critique claims such as “stationary means no forces” or “constant speed requires a forward net force,” then revise using the unit model.
ordered_flow.purpose: This is the section’s highest-value synthesis move; attach a canonical flawed-model figure for evidence-based critique.

retained_images.alt_text: Flawed force diagram for a cart rolling at constant speed
retained_images.purpose: Give Section 1.5 an authentic model-critique target tied to motion evidence and balanced/unbalanced force reasoning.

ordered_flow.notes: Extra course figure is permitted because this is explicitly a synthesis/application section and the figure directly serves the model-critique I-can.

ordered_flow.concept: Critique an incorrect force model and state the corrected force acting on the system.

ordered_flow.discussion_job: Use motion evidence to diagnose a force-model mismatch and propose a revision.
ordered_flow.prompt_skeleton: What feature of the flawed cart model conflicts with the stated constant-speed motion? What should be revised so the model and motion evidence agree?
expected_reasoning_evidence_to_listen_fo: Students identify the system before revising forces.
Students connect constant velocity to zero net force.
Students revise the diagram/claim rather than merely saying it is wrong.

summary_targets: A force model begins by defining the system and including only forces acting on that object.
Force arrows represent interactions with direction and relative magnitude; together they determine net force.
Balanced forces mean zero net force and unchanged motion; unbalanced forces mean motion changes.
A good force model must agree with the observed motion/evidence and can be revised when it does not.
common_mistakes_targets: Including a force the chosen object exerts on something else.
Omitting support force or weight from supported-object models.
Matching a constant-velocity description to an unbalanced force diagram.
Critiquing a model without naming the physical evidence or rule that makes it inconsistent.
